title: Deep Residual Injection for Full-Spectrum Forensic Signal Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models
claim: Naively fine-tuning a model on low-level cues conflicts with its semantic knowledge; injecting low-level signals as a residual into middle layers avoids this.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, naive conflict vs. residual-injection flow with fire/snowflake icons
description: Two side-by-side panels with large handwritten-style titles. The left panel, "Previous Methods" with a pink "Naive Training" label, shows a single blue MLLM box with a fire icon (trainable). Below it, a dashed pink box holds "Semantic" and "Low-Level" pills with crossed swords and a red "Conflict" label, plus a yellow warning triangle. The right panel, "Ours (Deep-VRM)", shows an orange Low-Level Encoder with a fire icon. Beside it is a light-blue MLLM Early Layers box with a snowflake (frozen), and a MLLM Later Layers box with a fire icon (trainable). A curved black arrow labeled "Residual Injection" leads to a "Low + Semantic" fusion bar between the early and later blocks. The eye goes first to the red "Conflict" text, then to the right-hand flow.
caption: Comparison between naively training MLLMs for detection and ours. While previous methods suffer from a representation conflict between semantic and low-level features, our approach decouples these two spaces via residual injection. It preserves established semantic knowledge while introducing artifact sensitivity to resolve the learning dilemma.
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have been increasingly adopted in forensics for their robust semantic understanding. As AI-generated images become realistic, semantic-level inconsistencies alone are often insufficient for reliable detection. This motivates a critical question: whether MLLMs can achieve full-spectrum forensic signal perception, i.e., capturing low-level generator artifacts without sacrificing pre-trained semantic knowledge. We further perform a layer-wise analysis of forensic signal perception in MLLMs, showing that semantic information is primarily formed in the early-to-middle layers, whereas direct fine-tuning for artifact learning disrupts these semantic representations. Based on this insight, we propose Deep Visual Residual MLLM (Deep-VRM) to preserve early semantic processing while injecting artifact-specific visual signals as a residual path into an intermediate layer, where they are fused with semantic token representations and propagated through subsequent trainable layers. This enables later layers to jointly model semantic reasoning and signal-level forensic cues, and surprisingly, the model learns to adaptively leverage different levels of forensic signals depending on the input, achieving robust and generalizable detection performance. Extensive experiments show that our method achieves state-of-the-art across most benchmarks. The code and data are available at https://github.com/KQL11/Deep-VRM.
